# What Is Seat-Based Pricing for AI?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-seat-based-pricing-for-ai/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Seat-based pricing charges a fixed fee for each named user of an AI tool, usually per month and often with an annual commitment. It is the standard model for AI assistants because it is easy to budget. Its weakness is that a seat measures access, not work: seats go unused, and an agent that works for many people does not fit the per-user model well.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## Key points

- Microsoft lists Microsoft 365 Copilot Business at $21.00 per user per month on annual billing, with a promotional $18.00 for the first year between 1 July and 31 December 2026.
- Anthropic lists Claude Team standard seats at $20 per seat per month billed annually or $25 monthly, with premium seats at $100 or $125.
- Seats are not unlimited: Anthropic's page says usage limits apply, and both vendors list metered or credit-based extras alongside the seat.
- Gartner said in July 2026 that agentic AI "breaks the link between user growth and revenue growth" for many software vendors.
- Deloitte's 2026 predictions expect hybrid models mixing licences with usage-, value- or outcome-based pricing to become standard.

## What seat-based pricing means

A seat is a licence for one named person. The buyer pays the same amount whether that person uses the tool every hour or never opens it. Most business AI assistants are sold this way, often with a cheaper rate for annual commitment.

Two vendor pages show the pattern. Prices below were checked on the vendors' own pages in November 2026 and change often.

| Plan | Annual billing | Monthly billing | Notes on the vendor page |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Microsoft 365 Copilot Business (add-on) | $21.00 per user per month; $18.00 promotional for the first year | $25.20 per user per month | Promotion runs 1 July to 31 December 2026; some features listed as "Metered" |
| Claude Team, standard seat | $20 per seat per month | $25 per seat per month | Teams of 2 to 150; usage limits apply |
| Claude Team, premium seat | $100 per seat per month | $125 per seat per month | "5x more usage than standard seats" |

The table shows two things that a headline seat price hides. Monthly billing costs 20% to 25% more per seat than the standard annual price on these plans. And a seat is no longer a flat entitlement. Anthropic's page says usage limits apply and that how fast a user reaches one "depends on the model you use, how long your chats are, and how large your files are". Microsoft's page lists some capabilities as metered. In practice many seat plans are already hybrids.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

The first issue is waste. A seat bought for someone with no defined task is a recurring cost with no return. Our analysis of AI assistants found that seats bought ahead of a workflow drift into low weekly use. The fix is to buy for the people in one commercial workflow and expand where use and results both move.

The second issue is structural. An agent does work on behalf of many people. If one agent drafts follow-ups for a whole sales team, charging per user undercharges for the work, and vendors know it. Gartner's July 2026 release put the point plainly: agentic AI "breaks the link between user growth and revenue growth for many enterprise software vendors". It estimated up to $234 billion of enterprise application spend exposed through 2030.

Deloitte's 2026 technology predictions draw the conclusion for buyers. It expects "subscriptions and seat-based licensing" could give way to hybrids, and that mixes of licences with "usage-, value-, or outcome-based pricing become standard". It cites Gartner's projection that by 2030 at least 40% of enterprise SaaS spend will shift toward usage-, agent- or outcome-based pricing.

For the buyer this means the seat price is the start of the cost, not the whole of it. Credits, metered agents and premium tiers sit beside it.

## How to buy seats well

| Check | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Name the workflow each seat serves | A seat without a task is the main source of waste |
| Compare annual and monthly billing | Annual is cheaper but locks in seats before use is proven |
| Read the usage limits and overage terms | Heavy users can hit limits or trigger metered charges |
| Separate assistant seats from agent costs | Agents are often priced by usage or credits, not seats |
| Track weekly active users per seat | The ratio shows whether to expand, hold or cut |
| Check promotional end dates | First-year discounts renew at list price |

Seats suit tools a person uses daily, where that person's time is the value. Usage or outcome pricing suits agents whose value scales with volume. Many firms will run both: seats for the assistant, metered pricing for the agents.

## lowob takeaways

- **A seat buys access, not work.** Value depends on whether the person has a task for it.
- **Seat plans are already hybrids.** Usage limits, credits and metered features sit beside the fee.
- **Agents strain the model.** One agent can serve many users, so vendors are moving to usage and outcomes.
- **Buy for a workflow.** Expand seat by seat on measured weekly use.

## Common questions

### What is seat-based pricing?

A pricing model that charges a fixed fee for each named user of a software tool, usually per month, regardless of how much each user uses it.

### Is seat-based or usage-based pricing better for AI?

Seats suit assistants a person uses daily. Usage suits agents whose work scales with volume. Many contracts now combine the two.

### Why are AI vendors moving away from per-seat pricing?

Agents can do work for many people, so user counts no longer track the value delivered. Gartner says this breaks the link between user growth and revenue growth.

### How many AI seats should a company buy?

Enough for the people in the first defined workflow. Expand as weekly use and the workflow's own results improve.
